2026 / Writing

Why this site uses posts

The decisions behind this site: one format for my work, a compact yearly index, and very little machinery.

My old homepage had a blog section and a list of achievements. It said surprisingly little about the work itself: what I built, which part I contributed, or why I made a particular choice. Adding more project names would not fix that.

I wanted one way to describe that work, whether it was a project, a small contribution, or a longer technical article. This post records the choices behind that structure.

One format, different amounts of detail

A project, an upstream fix, and a technical article can all be posts. Each gets a stable page with enough context to answer: what was the problem, what did I do, and where can you inspect the result? A small contribution might need two paragraphs and a pull-request link. A larger project can justify a longer explanation.

The alternative was separate sections for projects, contributions, achievements, and blogs. That would make me decide where something belongs before writing about it. One format avoids that bookkeeping. It does cost more effort than dropping a repository link onto a page; the explanation is the part worth spending that effort on.

Chronology is useful, but it is not a ranking

The index is grouped by year. I want to show how my work has developed, not turn the site into an activity feed. Years are enough for that. They also avoid giving a retrospective project note a precise publication date it never had.

The homepage continues from my introduction into a compact list of posts. The trade-off is that older work sits farther down the page. Year headings keep that work easy to locate.

Keep the machinery smaller than the content

The site serves plain HTML and CSS. A small Python script generates the indexes and post pages from a shared content file. There is no client-side router, and reading or following a link does not require JavaScript.

The trade-off is explicit: editing a post requires regenerating the pages. For this small collection, that seems preferable to maintaining an application just to publish text. The visual design follows the same choice: a white background, familiar links, and no decorative panels.

I got inspired by Russ Cox’s website.
